tasks.title: Science for everyone
tasks.instructions: For questions 1–8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
tasks.text:
Not so long ago, the idea that amateurs could make a meaningful contribution to scientific research would have been {{1}} as wishful thinking. Today, however, millions of volunteers around the world are {{2}} forces with professional researchers, classifying galaxies, counting birds and transcribing centuries-old weather logs. This army of enthusiasts has made discoveries that have taken specialists entirely by {{3}}: one volunteer spotted a previously unknown type of astronomical object while browsing telescope images in her spare time.

Critics initially {{4}} doubts about the reliability of data gathered by untrained observers. Such concerns are not without {{5}}, yet project designers have found ingenious ways of addressing them, for instance by having each image examined by dozens of people and {{6}} weight only to answers on which most agree. The result is data whose accuracy often {{7}} that of a single expert.

Perhaps the greatest benefit, though, is less tangible. Participants frequently report that the experience has {{8}} their understanding of how science actually works – messy, collaborative and endlessly provisional.

why.en: We 'dismiss something as' worthless or unrealistic – the verb takes 'as'. 'Ignored' and 'overlooked' mean 'not noticed' and cannot be followed by 'as + description'; 'denied' needs a that-clause or an object, not 'as'.
why.bg: Казваме 'dismiss something as' – отхвърляме нещо като несериозно; глаголът върви с 'as'. 'Ignored' и 'overlooked' значат 'не забелязвам' и не се използват с 'as + описание', а 'denied' иска обект или that-изречение.

why.en: 'Join forces (with)' is a fixed phrase meaning 'work together'. 'Linking' sounds possible because it also means connecting, but 'link forces' is not an English expression.
why.bg: 'Join forces (with)' е устойчив израз – обединявам усилия с някого. 'Linking' звучи логично, защото също значи 'свързвам', но 'link forces' просто не се казва.

why.en: The fixed phrase is 'take somebody by surprise'. 'Shock', 'amazement' and 'astonishment' are close in meaning, but none of them forms this expression.
why.bg: Устойчивият израз е 'take somebody by surprise' – изненадвам някого. 'Shock', 'amazement' и 'astonishment' са близки по смисъл, но не се използват в този израз.

why.en: We 'raise doubts' (= express them). 'Rose' is the tempting trap: it is the past of the intransitive verb 'rise' and cannot take an object such as 'doubts'. 'Lifted' is physical and 'grew' does not collocate here.
why.bg: Казваме 'raise doubts' – изказвам съмнения. Капанът е 'rose': това е минало време на 'rise', който е непреходен и не може да има обект като 'doubts'. 'Lifted' е физическо вдигане, а 'grew' не се съчетава така.

why.en: 'Not without foundation' means 'with some justification'. 'Ground' is tempting because we say 'there are grounds for concern', but that needs the plural and a different structure; 'not without ground' is not used.
why.bg: 'Not without foundation' значи 'не е съвсем без основание'. 'Ground' изкушава, защото казваме 'there are grounds for concern', но там е в множествено число и в друга конструкция; 'not without ground' не се казва.

why.en: We 'attach weight/importance to' something. 'Awarding' collocates with prizes and marks, 'conferring' with titles or degrees, and 'bearing weight' means physically supporting it.
why.bg: Казваме 'attach weight/importance to' – придавам значение на нещо. 'Awarding' върви с награди и оценки, 'conferring' – с титли и степени, а 'bearing weight' е буквално 'нося тежест'.

why.en: 'Rival' as a verb means 'be as good as': the data is as accurate as an expert's. 'Challenges' suggests questioning or competing, not equalling; 'contends' is intransitive (contend with); 'opposes' means 'is against'.
why.bg: Глаголът 'rival' значи 'съперничи, не отстъпва на': данните са толкова точни, колкото тези на експерт. 'Challenges' значи 'оспорва', а не 'равнява се на'; 'contends' иска 'with', а 'opposes' значи 'противопоставя се'.

why.en: 'Deepen your understanding' is the standard collocation. 'Enlarged' is tempting because it suggests growth, but we enlarge photos or rooms, not understanding.
why.bg: 'Deepen your understanding' е стандартната колокация – задълбочавам разбирането си. 'Enlarged' изкушава, защото носи идея за растеж, но уголемяваме снимки или стаи, не разбиране.

tasks.title: The power of a sugar pill
tasks.instructions: For questions 9–16, read the text below and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.
tasks.text:
The placebo effect – the improvement in symptoms that patients experience after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient – has long been regarded {{9}} something of a nuisance by medical researchers. After {{10}}, if a sugar pill can make people feel better, how is one to tell whether a new drug genuinely works? Increasingly, though, scientists are coming to see the phenomenon as worthy of study in {{11}} own right.

What makes the effect so intriguing is that it appears to depend {{12}} much on context as on chemistry. Expensive-looking pills, for instance, tend to outperform cheap ones, and injections generally outperform tablets, even when neither contains any active ingredient. More surprising still is the finding that placebos can work even when patients are fully aware {{13}} what they are taking. {{14}} researchers had expected such 'open-label' placebos to fail, a number of trials have shown modest benefits for conditions such as chronic back pain.

None of this means that doctors should start prescribing dummy pills. {{15}} it does suggest, however, is that the rituals surrounding medical care – the consultation, the reassurance, the sense of being looked {{16}} – may matter more than we think.

why.en: 'Regard something as something' – the verb 'regard' needs 'as' before the description. Without it the sentence is ungrammatical.
why.bg: 'Regard something as something' – глаголът 'regard' изисква 'as' пред описанието. Без него изречението е неграмотно.

why.en: 'After all' introduces a reason that supports the previous point. It's a fixed phrase – 'after this' or 'after that' would wrongly suggest a sequence in time.
why.bg: 'After all' въвежда довод, който подкрепя казаното – 'в крайна сметка'. Устойчив израз е; 'after this' би значело 'след това' във времето.

why.en: 'In its own right' = considered on its own merits. The possessive refers back to 'the phenomenon', so 'its' (not 'it's', which means 'it is').
why.bg: 'In its own right' = само по себе си, заслужено. Притежателното местоимение се отнася към 'the phenomenon', затова 'its' (не 'it's', което е 'it is').

why.en: 'As much on context as on chemistry' – the second 'as' in the text shows that this is an 'as … as' comparison. 'So' is only possible after a negative (not so much … as).
why.bg: 'As much on context as on chemistry' – второто 'as' в текста показва, че е сравнение 'as … as'. 'So' е възможно само след отрицание (not so much … as).

why.en: 'Aware of' – the adjective takes 'of', also before a wh-clause (aware of what…). 'About' is a common mistake here.
why.bg: 'Aware of' – прилагателното върви с 'of', включително пред въпросително изречение (aware of what…). 'About' е честа грешка тук.

why.en: A concession linker is needed: researchers expected failure, yet the trials showed benefits. 'Although/Though/While' all work. 'Despite' is wrong because it can't introduce a full clause.
why.bg: Трябва отстъпителен съюз: изследователите очаквали провал, но опитите показали ефект. Стават 'Although/Though/While'. 'Despite' не става, защото не може да въвежда цяло изречение.

why.en: A cleft sentence: 'What it does suggest … is that …'. 'What' means 'the thing that' and is the subject of 'is'. 'That' or 'which' can't start this kind of clause.
why.bg: Цепено изречение: 'What it does suggest … is that …'. 'What' значи 'това, което' и е подлог на 'is'. 'That' или 'which' не могат да започнат такова изречение.

why.en: 'Look after' = take care of, so 'the sense of being looked after' = feeling cared for. 'Looked at' is grammatical but loses the idea of care that fits 'reassurance'.
why.bg: 'Look after' = грижа се за, т.е. 'усещането, че някой се грижи за теб'. 'Looked at' е граматически възможно, но губи идеята за грижа, която пасва на 'reassurance'.

tasks.title: In defence of boredom
tasks.instructions: For questions 17–24, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
tasks.text:
For most of us, boredom is something to be avoided at all costs. The moment we feel the first signs of {{17}} (REST), we reach for our phones. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this {{18}} (WILLING) to tolerate even a few minutes of idleness may be costing us dearly.

In one widely cited experiment, participants who had first completed a deliberately {{19}} (TEDIUM) task – copying numbers from a telephone directory – went on to produce more {{20}} (IMAGINE) ideas in a subsequent creativity test than those who had not. Psychologists believe that boredom acts as a kind of signal, prompting the mind to wander and to make {{21}} (EXPECT) connections between ideas.

This is not to say that boredom is {{22}} (VARY) beneficial. Chronic boredom has been linked to poor mental health and risky behaviour. The key, researchers argue, lies in the {{23}} (DISTINGUISH) between brief, occasional lulls and a persistent sense that life lacks meaning. Learning to sit with the former, rather than {{24}} (REFLEX) reaching for a screen, may be one of the simplest ways to rediscover our creative potential.

why.en: Two suffixes: rest → restless (adj) → restlessness (noun). A noun is needed after 'signs of'. 'Rest' alone would mean the opposite.
why.bg: Две наставки: rest → restless (прил.) → restlessness (същ.). След 'signs of' трябва съществително. Само 'rest' би значело обратното.

why.en: After 'this' we need a noun, and the meaning is negative (we can't tolerate idleness): un- + willing + -ness. 'Willingness' would reverse the meaning.
why.bg: След 'this' трябва съществително, а смисълът е отрицателен (не понасяме бездействие): un- + willing + -ness. 'Willingness' обръща смисъла.

why.en: An adjective describing 'task': tedium (noun) → tedious. Watch the spelling: the -um ending is dropped.
why.bg: Прилагателно, което описва 'task': tedium (същ.) → tedious. Внимавай с правописа: окончанието -um отпада.

why.en: 'Imaginative ideas' = creative, original ideas. 'Imaginary' (= not real) is the classic trap: imaginary ideas would be ideas that don't exist.
why.bg: 'Imaginative ideas' = творчески, оригинални идеи. Класическият капан е 'imaginary' (= въображаем, несъществуващ).

why.en: Boredom helps the mind make surprising links, so we need the negative adjective: un- + expect + -ed. 'Expected' contradicts the idea of creativity.
why.bg: Скуката помага на ума да прави изненадващи връзки, затова трябва отрицателно прилагателно: un- + expect + -ed. 'Expected' противоречи на идеята за креативност.

why.en: An adverb modifying 'beneficial', meaning 'always': in- + vari- + -ably. 'Variably' is a real word but would mean 'to differing degrees', which doesn't fit 'This is not to say…'.
why.bg: Наречие към 'beneficial' със значение 'винаги': in- + vari- + -ably. 'Variably' съществува, но значи 'в различна степен' и не пасва на 'This is not to say…'.

why.en: 'The distinction between A and B' – the noun from 'distinguish' changes its ending to -tion. 'Distinguishing' is grammatical but not the standard noun used with 'between'.
why.bg: 'The distinction between A and B' – съществителното от 'distinguish' сменя окончанието си на -tion. 'Distinguishing' е граматически възможно, но не е стандартното съществително с 'between'.

why.en: An adverb describing how we reach for a screen: reflex → reflexive → reflexively (automatically, without thinking).
why.bg: Наречие, което описва как посягаме към екрана: reflex → reflexive → reflexively (машинално, без да мислим).

tasks.title: Key word transformations 1
tasks.instructions: For questions 25–30, complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between three and six words, including the word given.

questions.first: I didn't realise how serious the situation was until I read the report.
questions.after: the report that I realised how serious the situation was.

why.en: A cleft sentence with 'It was only when/after … that …' focuses on the moment of realisation. One mark for 'only when/after', one for 'I (had) read' or 'reading'. Don't write 'until' here: 'It was until…' is wrong.
why.bg: Цепено изречение 'It was only when/after … that …' поставя акцент върху момента на осъзнаването. Една точка за 'only when/after', една за 'I (had) read' или 'reading'. Не пиши 'until': 'It was until…' е грешно.

questions.first: The minister had no idea that the documents had been leaked.
questions.after: that the documents had been leaked.

why.en: Negative adverbials like 'Little' at the start trigger inversion: Little + did + subject + base verb. A common error is 'Little the minister knew' (no inversion) or 'Little did the minister knew' (past form after 'did').
why.bg: Отрицателни наречия като 'Little' в началото изискват инверсия: Little + did + подлог + основна форма. Честа грешка е 'Little the minister knew' (без инверсия) или 'did … knew' (минало време след 'did').

questions.first: People believe that the painting was stolen by a former employee.

why.en: Passive reporting structure: subject + is believed + perfect infinitive. Belief is present ('is believed'), the theft is past, so 'to have been (stolen)'. 'Was believed to be' changes both times.
why.bg: Безличен страдателен залог: подлог + is believed + перфектен инфинитив. Мнението е сега ('is believed'), а кражбата е в миналото, затова 'to have been (stolen)'. 'Was believed to be' сменя и двете времена.

questions.first: It was a mistake not to listen to your advice about the contract.
accept: wish that I had listened to

why.en: Regret about the past = wish + past perfect. 'I wish I listened' refers to the present, so it loses a mark. Remember 'listen to'.
why.bg: Съжаление за миналото = wish + минало перфектно време. 'I wish I listened' се отнася за настоящето и губи точка. Не забравяй 'listen to'.

questions.first: Rachel felt extremely nervous before her interview.

why.en: The idiom is 'have butterflies in your stomach' = feel nervous. Both halves are needed: the verb + 'butterflies', and 'in her stomach'. 'Had butterflies' alone is incomplete.
why.bg: Идиомът е 'have butterflies in your stomach' = имам пеперуди в стомаха, т.е. притеснен съм. Трябват и двете части: глагол + 'butterflies' и 'in her stomach'.

questions.first: Without your support, we would never have finished the project on time.
questions.after: your support, we would never have finished the project on time.

why.en: 'Had it not been for' = if it hadn't been for – a third conditional with inversion instead of 'if'. 'Had not it been for' and 'If it had not been for' (no keyword position) are wrong.
why.bg: 'Had it not been for' = ако не беше – трето условно с инверсия вместо 'if'. 'Had not it been for' е грешен словоред.

tasks.title: In praise of forgetting
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article about memory. For questions 31–36, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
tasks.text:
In praise of forgetting

For most of my adult life I regarded my memory as a faithful but slightly lazy servant. It kept the important things – birthdays, passwords, the plot of every novel I had ever taught – and let the trivia slip quietly away. When it failed me, I blamed fatigue or age, and resolved to try harder. It did not occur to me that forgetting might be something my brain was doing on purpose.

That idea, which once would have been dismissed as a convenient excuse, is now gaining ground among neuroscientists. For over a century the dominant model treated memory as a kind of storehouse: experiences were deposited, and forgetting was simply what happened when the deposits decayed or the filing system broke down. Forgetting, in this view, was a malfunction, and the goal of research was to understand – and ideally prevent – it. The newer view turns this on its head. Forgetting, its proponents argue, is an active process, carried out by dedicated mechanisms in the brain, and it exists for good reason.

The reasoning is disarmingly simple. A brain that retained everything would be hopelessly cluttered. Imagine trying to remember where you parked this morning if every previous parking space you had ever used were equally vivid. The ability to let go of outdated detail is precisely what allows us to act on what is current. More than that, forgetting the specifics of individual experiences seems to help us extract the general patterns that underlie them. A child who remembered every single dog she had met, in perfect detail, might struggle to form the concept 'dog' at all.

There is something deeply consoling in this. I confess that when I first came across the research, I read it with the relief of a defendant hearing the charges dropped. All those forgotten names at parties, the lost thread of an anecdote halfway through telling it – perhaps these were not symptoms of decline but signs of a well-run system doing its housekeeping. Yet the more I read, the more I suspected that I was drawing exactly the comfort I wanted from it, which is rarely a reliable basis for drawing conclusions. The scientists themselves are careful to distinguish between the kind of forgetting that serves us and the kind that does not. Losing track of where you parked last Tuesday is one thing; losing the ability to recognise your own children is quite another, and nobody is suggesting that the latter is adaptive.

What the research does challenge is a particular cultural attitude. We live in an age that fetishises total recall. Our phones photograph every meal; our email archives stretch back decades; entire industries exist to ensure that nothing, once recorded, is ever lost. We tend to regard this as an unambiguous gain, an extension of our fallible biological memory. But if forgetting has a function, then outsourcing our memories to machines that never forget may not be the unalloyed blessing it appears. Anyone who has been ambushed by an old photograph in a social media 'memories' feed – a former partner, a friend who has since died – will know that the past does not always return at a moment of our choosing.

None of this means we should start deleting our photo libraries. But it might prompt us to reconsider the anxious effort so many of us devote to remembering. I used to keep elaborate notebooks of everything I read, terrified that an insight might slip away. These days I am more relaxed. If an idea is important, I have found, it tends to resurface, often in a form more useful than the original because it has been stripped of irrelevant detail along the way. Whether that is the brain's forgetting mechanisms at work or simply the natural selectiveness of interest, I cannot say.

What I can say is that I no longer treat each lapse as a small catastrophe. My memory, it turns out, is less a lazy servant than a discerning editor – one whose judgement I am slowly learning to trust, even if I do not always agree with its choices.

questions.question: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that she had previously
options: been unaware that her memory kept some things and not others.
underestimated how much she depended on her memory.
assumed her lapses of memory had an obvious explanation.
been unusually confident about her ability to remember.

why.en: She 'blamed fatigue or age' and never imagined forgetting could be deliberate – so she took a simple cause for granted. A is wrong: she already knew her memory 'let the trivia slip quietly away', so she was aware it was selective.
why.bg: Тя 'blamed fatigue or age' и не е допускала, че забравянето може да е умишлено – т.е. приемала е проста причина. A е грешно: тя знае, че паметта ѝ 'let the trivia slip quietly away', значи е наясно, че е избирателна.

questions.question: According to the second paragraph, the traditional model of memory
options: treated forgetting as a sign that something had gone wrong.
was abandoned because it lacked sufficiently convincing evidence.
confused the storing of memories with their retrieval.
was originally intended only as a temporary explanation.

why.en: In the old 'storehouse' model, forgetting happened when deposits 'decayed' or the system 'broke down' – it was 'a malfunction'. B is tempting because the model has been replaced, but the text never says why it lost favour or mentions a lack of evidence.
why.bg: В стария модел 'склад' забравянето става, когато нещо се 'decayed' или 'broke down' – то е 'a malfunction'. B изкушава, защото моделът е изместен, но текстът не казва защо и не споменава липса на доказателства.

questions.question: What point does the writer make with the example of the child and the dogs?
options: Children's memories tend to be more detailed than adults'.
Losing detail can make it easier to grasp general ideas.
Concepts are learned most effectively through repetition.
Vivid old memories can interfere with recent ones.

why.en: The example follows 'forgetting the specifics … helps us extract the general patterns': a child who remembered every dog might not form the concept 'dog'. D is the trap – it describes the parking example earlier in the paragraph, not the dogs.
why.bg: Примерът идва след 'forgetting the specifics … helps us extract the general patterns': дете, което помни всяко куче, може да не формира понятието 'куче'. D е капан – то описва примера с паркирането, а не с кучетата.

questions.question: In the fourth paragraph, the writer admits that
options: she was at first sceptical about the research findings.
scientists have tended to overstate the value of forgetting.
her own memory problems were worse than she had believed.
her reaction to the research may have been wishful thinking.

why.en: She suspected she was 'drawing exactly the comfort I wanted from it' – i.e. believing what she hoped to believe. A is the opposite: she reacted with 'relief', not scepticism. B is wrong because the scientists are described as 'careful'.
why.bg: Тя подозира, че 'drawing exactly the comfort I wanted from it' – т.е. вярва на това, което ѝ се иска. A е обратното: реакцията ѝ е 'relief', не скептицизъм. B е грешно, защото учените са описани като 'careful'.

questions.question: What does the writer imply about digital technology in the fifth paragraph?
options: It can confront people with the past against their wishes.
It has made people careless about preserving their memories.
It is less reliable than human memory in the long term.
It has encouraged too much interest in other people's lives.

why.en: Being 'ambushed by an old photograph' shows that the past 'does not always return at a moment of our choosing'. B reverses the point: the paragraph says we keep everything, not that we are careless about it.
why.bg: Да те 'ambushed by an old photograph' показва, че миналото 'does not always return at a moment of our choosing'. B обръща смисъла: абзацът казва, че пазим всичко, а не че сме небрежни.

questions.question: How does the writer feel about her memory at the end of the article?
options: resigned to the fact that it is becoming less reliable
amused rather than troubled by its occasional failures
determined to find new ways of improving its performance
increasingly trusting, though with some reservations

why.en: She is 'slowly learning to trust' its judgement 'even if I do not always agree with its choices' – trust with some reservations. B is tempting because she no longer sees lapses as catastrophes, but nothing suggests she finds them amusing.
why.bg: Тя 'slowly learning to trust' преценката на паметта си, 'even if I do not always agree with its choices' – доверие с известни резерви. B изкушава, защото вече не вижда пропуските като катастрофа, но нищо не показва, че ѝ е забавно.

tasks.title: Learning through play?
tasks.instructions: You are going to read four extracts in which education specialists give their views on gamification – the use of game elements such as points and badges in learning. For questions 37–40, choose from the specialists A–D. The specialists may be chosen more than once.

texts.author: Dr Hannah Whitlock, educational psychologist
texts.text: Few educational trends have been embraced as eagerly as gamification. It is easy to see the appeal: in classroom trials, students' engagement typically shoots up the moment the first points are awarded. What enthusiasts tend to gloss over is how quickly that engagement fades once the novelty has worn off, usually within a matter of weeks. More troubling still is what happens to students' relationship with the subject itself. When pupils learn to solve equations in order to earn a badge, the badge rather than the mathematics becomes the point, and there is good reason to fear that their curiosity withers when the rewards stop. None of this means games have no place in schools, but they only work when a skilled teacher weaves them into a broader plan. Unfortunately, the studies cited in favour of gamification are mostly small and brief, and tell us little about these deeper effects.

texts.author: Marcus Oyelaran, secondary school head teacher
texts.text: Critics of gamification often caricature it as a crude system of bribes. In fact, the best-designed programmes are far subtler. Rather than rewarding mere participation, they build in genuine challenge, meaningful choice and a sense of progression, and when these elements are present the motivational benefits persist well beyond the initial excitement. I have seen students who once dreaded science become absorbed in it, precisely because a game gave them a way in; far from crowding out an interest in the subject, a well-made game can kindle one. That said, no platform runs itself. The teacher's role in setting goals, interpreting results and knowing when to switch the game off is, if anything, more important than before. The evidence for all this is now substantial: large, carefully controlled studies conducted over whole school years have produced consistent results, and it is no longer credible to dismiss gamification as a passing fad.

texts.author: Professor Ingrid Saarinen, learning technologist
texts.text: Anyone who has watched a class respond to a new learning app will recognise the pattern: a burst of enthusiasm, followed by a gradual return to business as usual once students have grown accustomed to it. Gamification is no exception, and its effect on motivation is, in my view, essentially a novelty effect. I am less persuaded by the argument that it damages pupils' interest in the subjects they study; I have seen little sign of that, and the claim seems to rest more on theory than on observation. What genuinely interests me is the potential of adaptive platforms to take over much of the routine work of encouraging and correcting students. Here, I suspect, the classroom teacher will become far less central than we are used to assuming, and that need not be a bad thing. It must be admitted, though, that the research so far is patchy, and much of it is funded by the companies selling the products.

texts.author: Leila Haddad, teacher trainer
texts.text: Gamification, done well, can sustain students' effort over a surprisingly long period. Programmes that let learners set their own targets and track their own improvement, rather than competing against classmates, seem to keep them engaged for months rather than weeks. My reservations lie elsewhere. However carefully designed, a system of external rewards sends students a message about why an activity is worth doing, and that message is not 'because history is fascinating'. I have known pupils who, once the points disappeared, simply lost interest in subjects they had previously enjoyed. Nor do I believe any software can substitute for a teacher who understands when a reward will help and when it will get in the way. As for the evidence, I would urge caution: much of it comes from short, small-scale studies, and the long-term picture remains largely unknown.

questions.question: Which specialist shares A's view on whether gamification's effect on motivation lasts?

why.en: A says engagement 'fades once the novelty has worn off'; C calls it 'essentially a novelty effect' followed by 'a return to business as usual'. B and D both say well-designed games keep students motivated for a long time.
why.bg: A казва, че интересът 'fades once the novelty has worn off'; C го нарича 'essentially a novelty effect'. B и D твърдят, че добре направените игри задържат мотивацията дълго.

questions.question: Which specialist has a different opinion from the others about the quality of the research into gamification?

why.en: B calls the evidence 'substantial', from 'large, carefully controlled studies'. A (studies 'small and brief'), C ('patchy', company-funded) and D ('short, small-scale') all doubt it.
why.bg: B нарича доказателствата 'substantial', от 'large, carefully controlled studies'. A ('small and brief'), C ('patchy', финансирани от фирмите) и D ('short, small-scale') се съмняват в тях.

questions.question: Which specialist expresses a similar view to D about the effect of rewards on students' interest in the subject itself?

why.en: D has seen pupils lose interest in subjects once the points disappeared; A fears 'their curiosity withers when the rewards stop'. C is the trap: C mentions this argument but is 'less persuaded' by it. B says games can 'kindle' interest.
why.bg: D е виждала ученици да губят интерес, щом точките изчезнат; A се опасява, че 'their curiosity withers when the rewards stop'. Капанът е C: споменава този аргумент, но е 'less persuaded'. B казва, че игрите могат да 'kindle' интерес.

questions.question: Which specialist takes a different view from the others on the role of the teacher?

why.en: C expects the teacher to 'become far less central' as platforms take over, and sees no harm in that. A, B and D all insist that a skilled teacher remains essential.
why.bg: C очаква учителят да 'become far less central', докато платформите поемат работата, и не вижда нищо лошо в това. A, B и D настояват, че опитният учител остава незаменим.

tasks.title: Listening to the ice
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article by a journalist who joined a scientific expedition to Antarctica. Six paragraphs have been removed from the article. Choose from the paragraphs A–G the one which fits each gap (41–46). There is one extra paragraph which you do not need to use.

options.text: That is precisely why Helen insists that every member of the team, however senior, spends at least an hour a day listening with nothing but their own ears. 'The software only finds what we've taught it to look for,' she told me. 'People still notice the things that don't fit.'

In the Southern Ocean, such disturbance remains relatively rare, which is what makes the team's recordings so valuable. They offer a baseline: a record of what an ocean sounds like before humans have filled it with noise, against which future changes can be measured.

It was this underwater soundscape that had brought me here, as a guest of a team of acoustic scientists spending six weeks recording it. Their instruments – hydrophones, essentially waterproof microphones – would be lowered over the side at intervals, sometimes for minutes, sometimes for days, to capture whatever the ocean had to say.

Humpback whales are the exception. Their songs, which can last for hours and evolve from one season to the next, have been studied so intensively that researchers can now tell individual singers apart. In these waters, however, they are summer visitors, and by the time we arrived most had already left.

'That's the ice,' she said quietly. 'It's melting from underneath, and that's the sound it makes as the water pours through.' Neither of us spoke for a while. I had come to the Antarctic expecting to hear the voices of whales. I left having heard, more clearly than I wanted to, the voice of a changing planet.

'Weddell seals,' she said, before I could ask. 'The whistles, anyway. The thudding we're still arguing about.' It was, I soon learned, a characteristic response. For all the sophistication of their equipment, the scientists were frank about how much of what they recorded remained unexplained.

Not that I was much use to science. On one occasion, I excitedly reported what I took to be a previously unknown animal call, only to be told, with great tact, that I had been listening to the ship's own engine. Still, the experience changed the way I thought about the ocean, which I had always pictured, rather vaguely, as a vast and empty space.

why.en: 'This underwater soundscape' refers back to the crackling and singing sea in the first paragraph, and C ends with 'whatever the ocean had to say', which the next paragraph picks up: 'What it had to say, as it turned out…'.
why.bg: 'This underwater soundscape' се връща към пращящото и пеещо море от първия абзац, а C завършва с 'whatever the ocean had to say', което следващият абзац подхваща: 'What it had to say, as it turned out…'.

why.en: 'Weddell seals,' she said answers the whistles in the recording Helen has just played. F ends on how much 'remained unexplained', and the next paragraph explains why: 'Part of the problem is sheer volume.'
why.bg: 'Weddell seals,' she said е отговор за свиренето в записа, който Хелън току-що е пуснала. F завършва с това колко 'remained unexplained', а следващият абзац обяснява защо: 'Part of the problem is sheer volume.'

why.en: 'That is precisely why' responds to the risk that unfamiliar sounds are 'overlooked' by software. The daily hour of listening in A is then picked up by 'My own hour of listening each day'. D is the trap: 'Humpback whales are the exception' has nothing to be an exception to here.
why.bg: 'That is precisely why' отговаря на риска софтуерът да 'overlooked' непознатите звуци. Часът слушане в A се подхваща от 'My own hour of listening each day'. Капанът е D: 'Humpback whales are the exception' няма на какво да е изключение тук.

why.en: 'Not that I was much use to science' follows the writer's enthusiasm for listening. G ends with the ocean as 'a vast and empty space', and the next paragraph contradicts this: 'The scientists … have known otherwise for decades.'
why.bg: 'Not that I was much use to science' следва ентусиазма на автора от слушането. G завършва с представата за океана като 'a vast and empty space', а следващият абзац я опровергава: 'The scientists … have known otherwise for decades.'

why.en: 'Such disturbance' refers to the human noise described in the previous paragraph, and B explains why the remote Southern Ocean recordings matter as a baseline.
why.bg: 'Such disturbance' се отнася към шума от човешка дейност в предишния абзац, а B обяснява защо записите от отдалечения Южен океан са ценни като отправна точка.

why.en: 'That's the ice,' she said explains the mysterious moan just described, and the closing reflection on a 'changing planet' gives the article its ending.
why.bg: 'That's the ice,' she said обяснява току-що описания мистериозен стон, а размисълът за 'a changing planet' завършва статията.

tasks.title: How I found my field
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article in which five scientists describe what drew them to their field. For questions 47–56, choose from the scientists (A–E). The scientists may be chosen more than once.

sections.heading: Ruth Adeyemi, marine biologist
sections.text: I grew up in a fishing town, and some of my earliest memories are of rock pools at low tide – crouching for hours over a few square metres of water, watching anemones open and close. I don't think I ever seriously considered doing anything else. My biology teacher at school was kind but rather uninspiring, to be honest; it was the sea itself that did the teaching. What nobody warns you about is how slowly things move. A single study of coral recovery can take a decade, and there are moments when I find that genuinely hard to bear, especially when the reefs I study are deteriorating faster than we can document them. But then I'll spend a morning diving and remember exactly why I'm here.

sections.heading: Marco Bellini, astrophysicist
sections.text: I was, frankly, a disaster at school. I daydreamed through most lessons and scraped through my exams, and nobody would have predicted I'd end up with a doctorate in anything. What changed was a second-hand telescope I bought with money from a summer job. I spent nights in the garden trying to find Saturn, failing, and eventually succeeding. People imagine astronomers as lone figures peering at the sky, but my working life is the opposite. A modern observatory project involves hundreds of people across a dozen countries, and the satisfaction of contributing a small piece to something so vast is, for me, the best part of the job. I'm not much given to predictions about where the field is heading – I leave that to others.

sections.heading: Sun-hee Park, neuroscientist
sections.text: I owe a great deal to Mrs Okonjo, who taught chemistry at my secondary school. She had a way of making every experiment feel like a mystery to be solved, and she was the one who persuaded me to apply for a science degree when I was leaning towards languages. I moved into neuroscience during my doctorate and have never looked back. It's an extraordinary moment to be in the field. The tools we now have for observing the living brain would have seemed like science fiction twenty years ago, and I'm convinced that within the next decade they will transform our understanding of conditions such as depression. My parents, both doctors, took it for granted that I would go into science, so there was never any drama about that.

sections.heading: Jonas Lindqvist, climate scientist
sections.text: I came to science late. For almost eight years I worked as an accountant, which paid well but left me feeling that I was watching life from the sidelines. A series of evening classes on weather and climate changed all that, and at thirty-one I gave up my job to study atmospheric physics. My background in numbers has been surprisingly useful. What I find hardest about the work is not the data or the long hours but the gulf between what the science says and what many people believe it says. I regularly meet people who are convinced that climate researchers simply design their models to suit an agenda, and however patiently I explain, it can be exasperating. I try not to let it discourage me.

sections.heading: Priya Raman, palaeogeneticist
sections.text: My parents had assumed I would join the family business, and when I announced that I wanted to study ancient DNA, there was a long, puzzled silence at the dinner table. I'm not sure they understood what it meant – I'm not sure I did either! I'd been fascinated by history since I was small, but I came to genetics more or less by chance: a lecturer I happened to sit next to on a train mentioned that her lab was looking for a research assistant, and I applied the following week. Had I taken a different train, I might be doing something entirely different now. The field moves at a remarkable speed – techniques I learned as a student are already outdated – and I find that exhilarating rather than daunting.

questions.statement: spent several years working in an unrelated profession

why.en: D worked 'as an accountant' for 'almost eight years'. C is the trap: she was only 'leaning towards languages' before university and never worked in another job.
why.bg: D е работил 'as an accountant' 'almost eight years'. Капанът е C: тя само 'leaning towards languages' преди университета и не е работила друго.

questions.statement: credits a particular teacher with influencing their decision

why.en: C says Mrs Okonjo 'persuaded me to apply for a science degree'. A also mentions a teacher, but calls them 'rather uninspiring'.
why.bg: C казва, че г-жа Оконджо 'persuaded me to apply for a science degree'. A също споменава учител, но го нарича 'rather uninspiring'.

questions.statement: admits to having performed poorly as a student

why.en: B: 'I was, frankly, a disaster at school … scraped through my exams.'
why.bg: B: 'I was, frankly, a disaster at school … scraped through my exams.' – признава, че е бил слаб ученик.

questions.statement: is frustrated by public misconceptions about their work

why.en: D describes 'the gulf between what the science says and what many people believe it says' as 'exasperating'. B mentions a popular image of astronomers but isn't frustrated by it.
why.bg: D описва 'the gulf between what the science says and what many people believe it says' като 'exasperating'. B споменава стереотип за астрономите, но не е раздразнен от него.

questions.statement: particularly values being part of a large team

why.en: B: contributing 'a small piece to something so vast' with 'hundreds of people' is 'the best part of the job'.
why.bg: B: да допринесеш 'a small piece to something so vast' заедно със 'hundreds of people' е 'the best part of the job'.

questions.statement: traces their interest back to early experiences in the natural world

why.en: A's 'earliest memories are of rock pools at low tide'. E was interested in history as a child, but that isn't the natural world; B's telescope came later, from a summer job.
why.bg: Най-ранните спомени на A 'are of rock pools at low tide'. E се интересува от история като дете, но това не е природата; телескопът на B идва по-късно.

questions.statement: acknowledges that chance played a part in their career

why.en: E came to genetics 'more or less by chance' after meeting a lecturer on a train: 'Had I taken a different train…'.
why.bg: E стига до генетиката 'more or less by chance' след среща с преподавателка във влака: 'Had I taken a different train…'.

questions.statement: sometimes finds the slow pace of progress hard to accept

why.en: A: a study 'can take a decade', and 'there are moments when I find that genuinely hard to bear'. E is the opposite: her field moves fast and she finds it 'exhilarating'.
why.bg: A: едно изследване 'can take a decade' и 'there are moments when I find that genuinely hard to bear'. E е обратното: полето ѝ се развива бързо и тя го намира за 'exhilarating'.

questions.statement: says their choice of career surprised their family

why.en: E's announcement was met with 'a long, puzzled silence at the dinner table' because her parents expected her to join the family business. C's parents 'took it for granted' – the opposite.
why.bg: Новината на E е посрещната с 'a long, puzzled silence at the dinner table', защото родителите ѝ са очаквали да влезе в семейния бизнес. Родителите на C 'took it for granted' – обратното.

questions.statement: makes a confident prediction about future developments in their field

why.en: C is 'convinced that within the next decade' new tools will transform our understanding of the brain. E says her field moves fast but predicts nothing; B explicitly avoids predictions.
why.bg: C е 'convinced that within the next decade' новите технологии ще променят разбирането ни за мозъка. E казва, че полето се развива бързо, но не прогнозира; B изрично избягва прогнози.

tasks.title: Why we put things off
tasks.instructions: For questions 1–8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
tasks.text:
Most of us have, at one time or another, put off an unpleasant task until the very last minute, only to {{1}} the consequences. For decades, procrastination was {{2}} down to poor time management or simple laziness. Recent research, however, paints a rather different picture. Psychologists now argue that putting things off is primarily a way of {{3}} with negative emotions such as anxiety or self-doubt: we avoid the task not because we cannot organise our time, but because thinking about it makes us feel bad.

This shift in perspective has important {{4}} for how the problem is tackled. Elaborate planners and productivity apps may be of little use if they fail to address the underlying feelings. Instead, researchers recommend that chronic procrastinators treat themselves with the same compassion they would {{5}} to a friend. In one study, students who forgave themselves for delaying revision before a first exam were markedly less {{6}} to do so before the next. Self-criticism, it {{7}} out, tends to deepen the very discomfort that drives avoidance in the first place. The key to breaking the cycle, then, may {{8}} not in iron discipline but in kindness.

why.en: 'Suffer the consequences' is the fixed collocation. 'Endure' is close in meaning but collocates with pain or hardship, and 'undergo' with operations or changes.
why.bg: 'Suffer the consequences' е устойчивата колокация – понасям последствията. 'Endure' е близко по смисъл, но върви с болка и трудности, а 'undergo' – с операции или промени.

why.en: 'Put something down to' means 'attribute it to a cause'. 'Laid down' exists but means 'established (rules)', and 'taken down' means 'written down' or 'removed'.
why.bg: 'Put something down to' значи 'отдавам нещо на някаква причина'. 'Laid down' съществува, но значи 'установявам правила', а 'taken down' – 'записвам' или 'свалям'.

why.en: Only 'cope' is followed by 'with' (cope with emotions). 'Handling', 'managing' and 'tackling' have the right meaning but are transitive: you handle emotions, not handle with them.
why.bg: Само 'cope' се използва с 'with' (cope with emotions). 'Handling', 'managing' и 'tackling' имат подходящ смисъл, но са преходни: казваш 'handle emotions', не 'handle with emotions'.

why.en: 'Implications for' = possible effects on. 'Applications' is the tempting option (it also takes 'for'), but it means practical uses, which doesn't fit 'a shift in perspective'.
why.bg: 'Implications for' = възможни последици за. Изкушава 'applications' (също върви с 'for'), но значи 'практически приложения', а това не пасва на 'промяна в гледната точка'.

why.en: We 'extend compassion/sympathy to' someone. 'Bestow' is formal and tempting, but it takes 'on/upon', not 'to'; 'lend' collocates with support or a hand, not compassion.
why.bg: Казваме 'extend compassion/sympathy to' някого. 'Bestow' е официално и изкушава, но върви с 'on/upon', не с 'to'; 'lend' се съчетава със 'support' или 'a hand', не с 'compassion'.

why.en: Only 'likely' can be followed by a to-infinitive with a person as subject (they were less likely to do so). 'Probable' has a similar meaning but needs 'it is probable that…'.
why.bg: Само 'likely' може да е последвано от инфинитив с 'to', когато подлогът е човек (they were less likely to do so). 'Probable' значи почти същото, но се казва 'it is probable that…'.

why.en: 'It turns out' (= it has been discovered) is the fixed parenthetical phrase. 'It works out' exists but means 'is resolved' or 'is calculated', not 'it emerges'.
why.bg: 'It turns out' (= оказва се) е устойчивият вметнат израз. 'It works out' съществува, но значи 'нещата се нареждат' или 'изчислява се', а не 'оказва се'.

why.en: 'The key lies in' is a fixed collocation. 'Rest' is the trap: we say something 'rests on' (depends on), but 'the key rests in' is not idiomatic.
why.bg: 'The key lies in' е устойчива колокация – ключът се крие в. Капанът е 'rest': казваме 'rests on' (зависи от), но 'the key rests in' не е естествено.

tasks.title: Taking the long way
tasks.instructions: For questions 9–16, read the text below and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.
tasks.text:
For most of the twentieth century, the appeal of air travel lay in its speed: the faster you reached your destination, the {{9}} time you had to enjoy it. A growing number of travellers, however, are now turning this logic on its head. Advocates of so-called 'slow travel' insist that the journey should be regarded not as an obstacle to be overcome, but as part and {{10}} of the experience itself.

Environmental concerns have undoubtedly played a part in this shift. Yet {{11}} motivates many slow travellers is not so much guilt about carbon emissions {{12}} a desire to reconnect with the places they pass through. Watching the landscape change gradually from a train window, they argue, gives a sense of distance that is {{13}} but impossible to achieve by air.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that slow travel is a luxury {{14}} only those with plenty of time and money can afford. {{15}} the cheapest rail fares often several times higher than budget airline tickets, and few employers willing to grant extra leave, it is hardly surprising that most holidaymakers continue to fly. Still, minority pursuit {{16}} it may be, slow travel seems set to change how many of us think about getting from one place to another.

why.en: 'The faster …, the more …' – a double comparative. 'Time' is uncountable, so 'more' (not 'most' or 'many').
why.bg: 'The faster …, the more …' – двойна сравнителна конструкция ('колкото…, толкова…'). 'Time' е неброимо, затова 'more' (не 'most' или 'many').

why.en: 'Part and parcel of' = an essential part of. It's a fixed idiom, so no other word works here.
why.bg: 'Part and parcel of' = неразделна част от. Това е устойчив идиом и друга дума не става.

why.en: 'What motivates many slow travellers is …' – a cleft structure where 'what' = 'the thing that'. 'That' or 'which' can't be used without a noun before them.
why.bg: 'What motivates many slow travellers is …' – цепено изречение, 'what' = 'това, което'. 'That' или 'which' не стават без съществително преди тях.

why.en: 'Not so much X as Y' = less X than Y. The pattern is fixed, so 'than' is wrong after 'so much'.
why.bg: 'Not so much X as Y' = не толкова X, колкото Y. Конструкцията е устойчива, затова 'than' след 'so much' е грешно.

why.en: 'All but impossible' = almost impossible. 'Nothing but' would mean 'only' and make no sense with 'impossible'.
why.bg: 'All but impossible' = почти невъзможно. 'Nothing but' би значело 'само' и няма смисъл с 'impossible'.

why.en: A defining relative clause after 'a luxury': 'a luxury that only those … can afford'. The relative pronoun is the object of 'afford'. 'What' is wrong because there is already a noun before the gap.
why.bg: Определително подчинено изречение след 'a luxury': 'a luxury that only those … can afford'. Относителното местоимение е допълнение на 'afford'. 'What' е грешно, защото преди празното място вече има съществително.

why.en: 'With + noun + adjective/participle' gives the reason or circumstances: 'With fares so high and few employers willing…'. There's no verb in this part, so a conjunction like 'since' or 'as' is impossible.
why.bg: 'With + съществително + прилагателно' дава причина или обстоятелство: 'При положение че цените са високи…'. В тази част няма глагол, затова съюз като 'since' или 'as' не става.

why.en: 'Minority pursuit though/as it may be' = although it may be a minority pursuit. The complement comes first for emphasis. 'Although' can't be used in this position.
why.bg: 'Minority pursuit though/as it may be' = макар и да е занимание за малцина. Допълнението е изнесено напред за акцент. 'Although' не може да се използва на тази позиция.

tasks.title: The empty office
tasks.instructions: For questions 17–24, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
tasks.text:
The mass shift to remote working in the early 2020s was {{17}} (PRECEDENT) in both its speed and its scale. Almost overnight, millions of office workers discovered that tasks once thought to require physical presence could be carried out just as {{18}} (EFFECT) from a kitchen table.

For city centres, the consequences have been far-reaching. Cafés and shops that relied on commuters have struggled to survive, and some commentators have predicted the {{19}} (EVITABLE) decline of the traditional business district. Others, however, dismiss such forecasts as {{20}} (ALARM). They point out that cities have reinvented themselves many times before, and that the {{21}} (VIBRANT) of urban life has never depended solely on office workers.

What seems clear is that the relationship between work and place is being {{22}} (DEFINE). Many employers now favour a hybrid model, which offers employees greater {{23}} (AUTONOMOUS) but brings challenges of its own, from scheduling meetings to maintaining a sense of team spirit. Whether this arrangement proves to be a {{24}} (TERM) solution or merely a transitional phase remains an open question.

why.en: Prefix and suffix together: un- + precedent + -ed = never seen before. A noun ('precedent') can't follow 'was' here with 'in both its speed…'.
why.bg: Представка и наставка заедно: un- + precedent + -ed = безпрецедентен. Съществителното 'precedent' не пасва след 'was' в това изречение.

why.en: An adverb after 'just as' describes how the tasks were carried out: effect → effective → effectively. 'Efficiently' comes from a different stem (EFFICIENT).
why.bg: Наречие след 'just as', което описва как се вършат задачите: effect → effective → effectively. 'Efficiently' е от друга основа (EFFICIENT).

why.en: 'The inevitable decline' = a decline that can't be avoided. The prefix is in-, not un-.
why.bg: 'The inevitable decline' = неизбежният упадък. Представката е in-, не un-.

why.en: To 'dismiss forecasts as alarmist' = say they exaggerate the danger. 'Alarming' (= worrying) is the trap: you wouldn't dismiss something because it is worrying.
why.bg: 'Dismiss forecasts as alarmist' = отхвърлям прогнозите като паникьорски, преувеличени. Капанът е 'alarming' (= тревожен) – не отхвърляш нещо, защото е тревожно.

why.en: After 'the … of urban life' we need a noun: vibrant → vibrancy. Verb agreement ('has') confirms a singular noun.
why.bg: След 'the … of urban life' трябва съществително: vibrant → vibrancy. Глаголът 'has' потвърждава единствено число.

why.en: A passive continuous needs a past participle, and the meaning is 'defined again in a new way': re- + define + -d. 'Defined' alone misses the idea of change.
why.bg: Продължителният страдателен залог иска минало причастие, а смисълът е 'определя се наново': re- + define + -d. Само 'defined' губи идеята за промяна.

why.en: After 'greater' we need a noun: autonomous → autonomy (independence). 'Autonomousness' is not used.
why.bg: След 'greater' трябва съществително: autonomous → autonomy (самостоятелност). 'Autonomousness' не се използва.

why.en: A compound adjective contrasting with 'a transitional phase': long-term. 'Short-term' is grammatical but contradicts the contrast with 'merely transitional'.
why.bg: Сложно прилагателно, което контрастира с 'a transitional phase': long-term. 'Short-term' е граматически възможно, но противоречи на контраста с 'merely transitional'.

tasks.title: Key word transformations 2
tasks.instructions: For questions 25–30, complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between three and six words, including the word given.

questions.first: A professional photographer is going to take our wedding photos.

why.en: Causative: have + object + past participle, when someone else does the job for you. The object must come before 'taken'; 'have taken our photos' means we took them ourselves.
why.bg: Каузатив: have + обект + минало причастие, когато някой друг върши работата вместо теб. Обектът трябва да е преди 'taken'; 'have taken our photos' значи, че сами сме ги снимали.

questions.first: Nobody had expected the council to make that decision.
accept: came as a complete surprise to
came as a total surprise to

why.en: The fixed phrase is 'come as a surprise to somebody'. Watch the article 'a' and the preposition 'to': 'came as surprise for everyone' loses both marks.
why.bg: Устойчивият израз е 'come as a surprise to somebody'. Внимавай с члена 'a' и предлога 'to': 'came as surprise for everyone' губи и двете точки.

questions.first: The constant noise from the building site irritates me more than anything else.
questions.after: the constant noise from the building site.
accept: What irritates me the most is
What I find most irritating is

why.en: A wh-cleft: What + clause + is + focus. 'More than anything else' = 'most'. Don't forget 'is' before the noise – it links the two halves.
why.bg: Цепено изречение с 'What': What + изречение + is + акцент. 'More than anything else' = 'most'. Не забравяй 'is' пред шума – то свързва двете части.

questions.first: 'You really should apply for the job, Tom,' said Lisa.

why.en: Reporting verb pattern: encourage + person + to-infinitive. 'Encouraged Tom applying' or 'encouraged that Tom should apply' are wrong patterns.
why.bg: Модел с глагол за преразказ: encourage + човек + инфинитив с 'to'. 'Encouraged Tom applying' или 'encouraged that Tom should apply' са грешни модели.

questions.first: I'm sure Mark didn't intend to offend anyone.

why.en: Negative deduction about the past: can't/couldn't + have + past participle. 'Mustn't have meant' is not used for deduction in British English, and 'didn't mean' loses the certainty.
why.bg: Отрицателно заключение за миналото: can't/couldn't + have + минало причастие. 'Mustn't have' не се използва за заключение, а 'didn't mean' губи увереността.

questions.first: The film was far less entertaining than I had expected.

why.en: 'Not nearly as … as' = much less … than. 'Nearly' must follow 'not', and the comparison needs 'as … as', not 'than'.
why.bg: 'Not nearly as … as' = далеч не толкова … колкото. 'Nearly' стои след 'not', а сравнението иска 'as … as', не 'than'.

tasks.title: Lost and found in translation
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article by a literary translator. For questions 31–36, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
tasks.text:
Lost and found in translation

People who discover what I do for a living tend to ask one of two questions. The first is how many languages I speak, which is easily answered. The second, usually posed with a slightly apologetic air, is whether my job will soon be done by machines. I used to bristle at this. Now I find it rather useful, because the honest answer obliges me to explain what translation actually involves – something I suspect even many keen readers of translated fiction have never stopped to consider.

The popular image of the translator is of a sort of human dictionary, swapping words in one language for their equivalents in another. If that were all there was to it, the machines would indeed have won long ago. But languages do not map neatly onto one another. Take a single adjective from the Portuguese novel I am working on at present: it describes a kind of afternoon light, and carries connotations of nostalgia, heat and faint boredom that no English word captures. I can choose a word that conveys the light and lose the mood, or one that conveys the mood and lose the light. Or I can rebuild the whole sentence so that the mood seeps in from elsewhere – which is what, after three days of dithering, I eventually did.

Decisions of this kind are the substance of the work, and they are never purely technical. They require a judgement about what matters most in a given passage, and that judgement rests on an understanding of the whole book: its rhythms, its jokes, its silences. A translator is, in this sense, the most attentive reader a novel will ever have. We cannot skim; we cannot skip the boring bits; we have to account for every comma. It is an intimacy that can be exhilarating and, with a poor book, faintly oppressive.

None of this is to dismiss machine translation, which I use myself for drafts of business correspondence and which is, for many purposes, astonishingly good. The difficulty arises when its fluency is mistaken for understanding. A machine produces the most statistically likely rendering of a sentence, and in literary prose the most likely rendering is very often the wrong one, precisely because good writers tend to avoid the obvious. A novelist who has spent years searching for an unexpected phrase deserves a translator who will not smooth it into a cliché.

What worries me more than the technology itself is the economic pressure that comes with it. Publishers, understandably anxious about costs, are increasingly offering translators the chance to 'post-edit' machine output for a fraction of the usual fee. The argument is that most of the work has already been done. In my experience the opposite is true: correcting a fluent but subtly wrong draft is often slower than starting from scratch, because the errors are camouflaged. Worse, the machine's choices have a way of anchoring one's own, so that the finished text drifts towards blandness without anyone quite noticing. If this becomes the norm, readers will gradually be offered a narrower, flatter version of world literature, and will not know what they are missing.

Translators, it must be said, have not always helped their own cause. For generations we were trained to be invisible, our names relegated to the small print, our contribution measured by how little the reader noticed it. That modesty was admirable in its way, but it made it easy for others to assume there was nothing much to notice. Recently, more publishers have begun putting translators' names on book covers, and some prizes now split their award between author and translator. These are small changes, but they reflect a dawning recognition that a translated novel is a collaboration, not a copy.

So, will my job be done by machines? Parts of it, perhaps. The drudgery of looking up obscure terms has already been eased, and I am not nostalgic for it. But the heart of the work – listening to a voice in one language and finding a way for it to speak in another – seems to me as stubbornly human as writing the book in the first place. I may, of course, be wrong. Translators are no better at predicting the future than anyone else. We are simply more used to living with uncertainty about whether we have got things right.

questions.question: How does the writer now feel about being asked whether machines will replace her?
options: She resents the suggestion that her work is simple and mechanical.
She sees it as a chance to explain what her work involves.
She suspects that the question is not meant seriously.
She finds it difficult to give a convincing answer.

why.en: 'Now I find it rather useful, because the honest answer obliges me to explain what translation actually involves.' A is the trap: she 'used to bristle' at the question, but that was in the past.
why.bg: 'Now I find it rather useful, because the honest answer obliges me to explain what translation actually involves.' Капанът е A: тя 'used to bristle', но това е било в миналото.

questions.question: The writer mentions the Portuguese adjective in order to illustrate
options: how rarely words correspond exactly across languages.
how long it can take to translate a single sentence.
how much richer Portuguese is than English in places.
how translators decide which meaning to sacrifice.

why.en: The example follows 'languages do not map neatly onto one another' and shows a word with no English equivalent. D is tempting, but in the end she avoided sacrificing either meaning by rebuilding the sentence; B is a detail (three days), not the purpose.
why.bg: Примерът идва след 'languages do not map neatly onto one another' и показва дума без английски еквивалент. D изкушава, но накрая тя не жертва нито едното значение – преправя изречението; B е детайл (три дни), а не целта.

questions.question: What does the writer suggest about a translator's relationship with a book?
options: It is closer than that of any other kind of reader.
It depends on sharing the author's sense of humour.
It becomes a burden when the book is especially long.
It requires ignoring the less interesting passages.

why.en: 'A translator is … the most attentive reader a novel will ever have' – an unusually close relationship. C is the trap: she says the intimacy can be 'oppressive' with a poor book, not a long one. D contradicts 'we cannot skip the boring bits'.
why.bg: 'A translator is … the most attentive reader a novel will ever have' – необичайно близка връзка. Капанът е C: тя казва, че близостта е 'oppressive' при слаба книга, не при дълга. D противоречи на 'we cannot skip the boring bits'.

questions.question: What is the writer's view of machine translation in the fourth paragraph?
options: It should only be relied on for business documents.
It is improving faster than translators like to admit.
It struggles with literature because it prefers the expected.
It is considerably less fluent than its supporters tend to claim.

why.en: Machines produce 'the most statistically likely rendering', which is often wrong in literature because 'good writers tend to avoid the obvious'. A is tempting because she uses it for business letters, but she also calls it 'astonishingly good' 'for many purposes'. D contradicts 'its fluency'.
why.bg: Машината дава 'the most statistically likely rendering', а в литературата това често е грешно, защото 'good writers tend to avoid the obvious'. A изкушава, защото тя я ползва за делова кореспонденция, но я нарича и 'astonishingly good' 'for many purposes'. D противоречи на 'its fluency'.

questions.question: The writer's main concern about 'post-editing' is that
options: translators will no longer be able to earn a living.
publishers are misleading readers about how translated books are made.
translators are not trained to correct machine errors.
translated fiction may become blander without anyone noticing.

why.en: The finished text 'drifts towards blandness without anyone quite noticing', so readers get 'a narrower, flatter version of world literature'. A is tempting because she mentions lower fees, but the consequence she stresses is the effect on literature, not on income.
why.bg: Готовият текст 'drifts towards blandness without anyone quite noticing' и читателите получават 'a narrower, flatter version of world literature'. A изкушава заради по-ниските хонорари, но тя набляга на последиците за литературата, а не за доходите.

questions.question: What does the writer say about the way translators have traditionally seen their role?
options: They resented being left off the covers of books.
They cared more about prizes than about recognition.
Their training failed to keep up with the publishing world.
Their modesty encouraged others to undervalue their work.

why.en: Being trained to be invisible 'made it easy for others to assume there was nothing much to notice'. A is wrong: the text says their names were in small print, but not that they resented it – in fact they accepted invisibility as a virtue.
why.bg: Това, че са били учени да са невидими, 'made it easy for others to assume there was nothing much to notice'. A е грешно: имената им са били с дребен шрифт, но текстът не казва, че са негодували – напротив, приемали са невидимостта за добродетел.

tasks.title: Letting the city grow wild
tasks.instructions: You are going to read four extracts in which writers give their views on 'rewilding' urban green spaces by mowing less and letting plants grow freely. For questions 37–40, choose from the writers A–D. The writers may be chosen more than once.

texts.author: Dr Elena Brandt, urban ecologist
texts.text: When our city stopped mowing a handful of roadside verges five years ago, the change in wildlife was visible within a single summer: wild flowers returned, and with them bees, butterflies and the birds that feed on them. Surveys since then have confirmed a striking increase in the number of species recorded. Not everyone was delighted at first. Complaints about 'neglect' poured in, and some residents were convinced the council was simply cutting corners. Yet once explanatory signs went up and the flowers came into bloom, opposition largely melted away. The financial case is equally persuasive: less frequent mowing has reduced maintenance bills considerably. I would not, however, want to see every park given over to long grass. People need places to picnic and play football, and rewilded patches work best as a complement to conventional green space rather than a substitute for it.

texts.author: Gareth Pryce, parks manager
texts.text: I have no quarrel with the principle of rewilding, but I think its advocates sometimes promise more than it can deliver. A strip of uncut grass between two busy roads is not a nature reserve, and the boost to biodiversity reported by some projects owes as much to optimistic counting as to any real ecological change. Residents, in my experience, are more open-minded than they are given credit for; a few grumble at first, but most accept the new look within a season or two. What does concern me is the widespread belief that rewilding saves money. Establishing and managing a genuinely diverse meadow requires specialist skills, seed and monitoring, and the costs can easily exceed those of routine mowing. Used selectively, alongside traditional parks, it has much to offer – but it should be sold honestly.

texts.author: Dr Amara Nwosu, sociologist
texts.text: The ecological benefits of urban rewilding are now well documented, and the savings councils make by mowing less are real, if modest. My research, however, has focused on how residents respond, and here the picture is less rosy than campaigners like to suggest. In the neighbourhoods we studied, hostility to 'messy' green spaces did not fade over time; if anything, it hardened, particularly among older residents for whom a neatly kept lawn signified a community that cared. Information campaigns made little difference. Unless projects involve local people from the outset, rather than presenting them with a finished plan, I fear rewilding will continue to be seen as something done to communities rather than with them. That is not an argument for abandoning it – wild areas and conventional parks can coexist perfectly well – but it is a warning.

texts.author: Tom Ellery, environmental campaigner
texts.text: We are in the middle of a biodiversity crisis, and cities have a part to play. The evidence that wilder green spaces support far more insects, birds and small mammals than closely mown grass is overwhelming. I would go further than many of my colleagues: the manicured lawn, which offers almost nothing to wildlife, should become the exception rather than the rule in our parks, with only small areas kept short for recreation. Some people will object, of course, though in my experience the initial outcry rarely lasts once residents see the results for themselves. I would caution, however, against selling rewilding as a cost-cutting measure. Done properly, it requires investment in planting, monitoring and education, and councils that adopt it purely to save money are likely to be disappointed.

questions.question: Which writer has a different view from the others about the benefits of rewilding for wildlife?

why.en: B thinks reported gains owe 'as much to optimistic counting as to any real ecological change'. A ('a striking increase'), C ('well documented') and D ('overwhelming') all accept the benefits.
why.bg: B смята, че отчетените ползи се дължат 'as much to optimistic counting as to any real ecological change'. A ('a striking increase'), C ('well documented') и D ('overwhelming') приемат ползите.

questions.question: Which writer shares B's opinion on the cost of rewilding compared with conventional maintenance?

why.en: B says costs 'can easily exceed those of routine mowing'; D warns against 'selling rewilding as a cost-cutting measure' because it 'requires investment'. A and C both say mowing less saves money.
why.bg: B казва, че разходите 'can easily exceed those of routine mowing'; D предупреждава да не се представя като 'a cost-cutting measure', защото 'requires investment'. A и C твърдят, че по-рядкото косене спестява пари.

questions.question: Which writer has a different opinion from the others on how local residents' attitudes change over time?

why.en: C found that hostility 'did not fade over time; if anything, it hardened'. A (opposition 'melted away'), B (most 'accept the new look') and D (the outcry 'rarely lasts') all say residents come round.
why.bg: C открива, че враждебността 'did not fade over time; if anything, it hardened'. A ('melted away'), B ('accept the new look') и D ('rarely lasts') казват, че хората свикват.

questions.question: Which writer disagrees with A about whether rewilded areas should largely replace conventional parkland?

why.en: A wants rewilding as 'a complement … rather than a substitute'; D wants the mown lawn to become 'the exception rather than the rule'. B ('alongside traditional parks') and C (they 'can coexist') agree with A.
why.bg: A иска дивите площи да са 'a complement … rather than a substitute'; D иска окосената трева да стане 'the exception rather than the rule'. B ('alongside traditional parks') и C ('can coexist') са съгласни с A.

tasks.title: The apple detective
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article about a man who searches for lost apple varieties. Six paragraphs have been removed from the article. Choose from the paragraphs A–G the one which fits each gap (41–46). There is one extra paragraph which you do not need to use.

options.text: That story, which he clearly enjoys telling, involved a single gnarled tree that had survived the construction of the car park because nobody had got round to removing it. Hartley noticed it while loading his shopping. When he returned in the autumn to collect fruit, a security guard demanded to know what he was doing. 'I told him I was saving a piece of history,' Hartley recalls. 'He didn't look convinced.'

He will not know for certain until the DNA results come back, which may take months. He does not seem to mind. 'The waiting is part of it,' he says, shouldering his bag. 'These trees have been patient for a hundred years. I can manage a few more weeks.'

It is that instinct, honed over years, that I see in action as we walk through an orchard on the edge of a small village. Hartley stops beside a tree, studies the shape of the fruit, cuts one open and examines the pattern of the seeds. He takes a bite and chews thoughtfully. 'Promising,' is all he will say.

His interest began, he tells me, almost by accident. Clearing the overgrown garden of a house he had just bought, he came across an ancient, lichen-covered tree that still produced a modest crop of small, russet-skinned fruit. Nobody could tell him what it was. 'That bothered me,' he says. 'Somebody had planted it, chosen it, cared for it. And its name had simply vanished.'

Commercial growers are not entirely to blame for this narrowing of choice. Supermarkets, keen to offer consistent produce all year round, have little interest in apples that bruise easily or keep for only a few weeks, and shoppers have grown used to fruit that looks the same whatever the season.

These are often frustratingly vague. A Victorian catalogue might describe an apple as 'of good flavour, medium size, ripening late' – a description that could apply to dozens of varieties. Hartley supplements them with paintings, old photographs and, increasingly, DNA analysis, which can confirm whether two trees share the same genetic identity.

But he is equally drawn by something harder to measure. Each variety, he says, embodies the choices of the people who grew it – the flavours they prized, the uses they had in mind, whether for eating, cooking or making cider. 'When a variety disappears, you lose a piece of how people lived.'

why.en: D tells how his interest began with one unidentified tree, and the next paragraph continues: 'The tree eventually turned out to be…'. No other option introduces a single tree.
why.bg: D разказва как интересът му започва с едно непознато дърво, а следващият абзац продължава: 'The tree eventually turned out to be…'. Никоя друга опция не въвежда едно конкретно дърво.

why.en: 'That story' refers to the 'memorable occasion' in the supermarket car park mentioned at the end of the previous paragraph.
why.bg: 'That story' се отнася към 'memorable occasion' на паркинга на супермаркета, споменат в края на предишния абзац.

why.en: 'These are often frustratingly vague' refers to the 'historical records'. F introduces DNA analysis, which the next paragraph qualifies: 'Yet even DNA has its limits.'
why.bg: 'These are often frustratingly vague' се отнася към 'historical records'. F въвежда ДНК анализа, който следващият абзац ограничава: 'Yet even DNA has its limits.'

why.en: 'It is that instinct' picks up 'a certain amount of instinct' at the end of the previous paragraph and shows it in action.
why.bg: 'It is that instinct' подхваща 'a certain amount of instinct' от края на предишния абзац и го показва в действие.

why.en: 'But he is equally drawn by something harder to measure' contrasts with the reason that is 'partly practical'. E is the trap: it could follow the mention of a few commercial varieties, but then G, which needs the 'partly practical' contrast, would have nowhere to go.
why.bg: 'But he is equally drawn by something harder to measure' контрастира с причината, която е 'partly practical'. Капанът е E: може да изглежда, че следва споменаването на малкото търговски сортове, но тогава G, който има нужда от контраста с 'partly practical', няма къде да отиде.

why.en: B follows the apples from a possible lost variety: 'He will not know for certain until the DNA results come back' refers to his 'hunch', and the quotation closes the article.
why.bg: B следва ябълките от евентуално изгубен сорт: 'He will not know for certain until the DNA results come back' се отнася към неговото 'hunch', а цитатът завършва статията.

tasks.title: My first failure
tasks.instructions: You are going to read an article in which four entrepreneurs talk about the first business they set up that failed. For questions 47–56, choose from the entrepreneurs (A–D). The entrepreneurs may be chosen more than once.

sections.heading: Lena Fischer – a zero-waste café
sections.text: Everyone told me the location was wrong. My accountant, my sister, even the estate agent who let me the premises hinted that a side street with almost no passing trade was a risky place for a café. I listened politely and signed the lease anyway, convinced that a good concept would draw people in. For a while, it did – the opening weeks were wonderful. The turning point came on a wet Tuesday in February, about a year in, when I sat at the counter from seven until three and served eleven customers. I remember doing the arithmetic on a napkin and knowing, with total clarity, that it was over; I just didn't admit it to anyone for another six months. When I finally handed back the keys, what I felt above all was a kind of lightness, as if I'd been holding my breath for a year and could finally exhale.

sections.heading: Kwame Asante – a fitness app
sections.text: I was so focused on building the product that I barely looked at what else was out there.
